cards.prompt: A support bot must answer from a product manual that changes every week. Answers must cite the page they came from. Which approach fits best?
choices: Retrieval-augmented generation over the manual
Fine-tune the model on the manual each week
Train a new model from scratch
A longer system prompt with no retrieval
cards.explanation: Facts that change and need citations belong in an index you can refresh and point at, not in weights. Retrieval lets you update a document in minutes and show the source. Fine-tuning is better for stable style or format, and a fixed prompt cannot hold a whole manual.

cards.prompt: You need every reply in a strict house JSON format and tone. A good prompt gets 82% of replies right, and you have 5,000 reviewed examples. What is the sensible next step?
choices: Add a retrieval index of the examples
Switch to a bigger base model and stop
Fine-tune on the reviewed examples
Lower the temperature to zero and ship
cards.explanation: Behaviour and format consistency are what fine-tuning is good at, and you already have labelled data. Retrieval supplies knowledge, not discipline. Temperature zero removes sampling variety but does not teach a format the model keeps missing.

cards.prompt: One GPU, a 7B-parameter model, and ten different customer-specific tasks to serve. Which fine-tuning plan is most practical?
choices: Ten separate full fine-tunes
One low-rank adapter (LoRA) per task on a shared frozen base
One full fine-tune on all tasks mixed with no task tags
Retrain the tokenizer for each customer
cards.explanation: Adapters train a small number of extra parameters, fit in far less memory, and can be swapped on one resident base model. Ten full copies multiply storage and serving cost. Full fine-tuning can still win on quality for a large domain shift, which is the deciding factor to measure.

cards.prompt: A fraud model sees 1 fraud in 1,000 transactions. A model that always predicts 'not fraud' reaches 99.9% accuracy. Which metric should you report instead?
choices: Accuracy, but on a bigger test set
Training loss
Mean squared error on the labels
Precision and recall (or PR-AUC) on the fraud class
cards.explanation: With rare positives accuracy mostly measures the base rate. Precision and recall look only at the positive class, and PR-AUC summarises the trade-off across thresholds.

cards.prompt: Trade-off duel: you double the batch size and scale the learning rate with it. Which statement is the honest summary?
choices: Training always gets faster and always generalises better
Each step is less noisy and hardware is used better, but very large batches can generalise worse unless tuned
Gradients become exact so no validation set is needed
Convergence per epoch is guaranteed to improve
cards.explanation: Bigger batches reduce gradient noise and improve throughput, yet the noise also acts as a mild regulariser, so past a point you may need warm-up, a retuned learning rate or more regularisation. Nothing makes validation unnecessary.

cards.prompt: Trade-off duel: an approximate nearest-neighbour index is 40x faster than exact search but misses some true neighbours. When is it the wrong call?
choices: When the corpus has millions of passages
When latency matters to users
When a missed document can cause a harmful wrong answer and the corpus is small enough to search exactly
When you can measure recall@k against exact search
cards.explanation: Approximate search trades recall for speed, which is a bargain at scale. On a small corpus exact search is cheap, so giving up recall buys nothing. Measuring recall@k against exact results is how you decide.

cards.prompt: An LLM judge scores two answers. Which known biases should you test for before trusting it? Pick all that apply.
choices: Preferring the answer shown first
Preferring longer answers
Preferring answers written by its own model family
Preferring answers with fewer typos in the question
cards.explanation: Position, length and self-preference are well-documented judge biases. Swap the order, control length, and calibrate against human labels. A judge is a measuring instrument, so you validate it like one.
